To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the use of cyclic backbone NGR-based imaging agents increases efficacy of postmyocardial infarction angiogenesis imaging.
the novel cyclic backbone NGR-based SPECT tracers coNGR and co(NGR4) are promising imaging agents for detection of angiogenic processes in infarct myocardium.

the novel coNGR peptides show a higher affinity for CD13 than the previously reported disulphide-cyclized NGR peptide, and that the co(NGR)-4 tetramer is the most promising imaging agent for detection angiogenesis in myocardial infarcted tissue.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of new imaging agents for the detection of angiogenesis after myocardial infarction.
the development of a novel imaging agent based on the CD13-targeting NGR motif.
the synthesis and evaluation of two new CD13-targeting imaging agents, coNGR and co(NGR), which are based on a cyclic backbone instead of a disulfide bridge.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the coNGR-based SPECT agents are superior to the previously described cNGR imaging agents in terms of in vitro and in vitro characteristics and therefore may have a potential to be applied for noninvasive imaging of angiogenesis in vivo.

co(NGR), a novel tetrameric CD13-targeting imaging agent, is more sensitive and specific for angiogenesis imaging in the postmyocardial infarction setting compared to previously reported NGR-based imaging agents.
the coNGR-based tracers have a better in vitro and in vivostability compared to cNGR and are promising imaging agents to detect angiogenic processes in infarct areas.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the novel coNGR peptides are promising imaging agents for detection of angiogenic processes and may have a potential in clinical practice.
the use of NCL for cyclization of NGR peptide-based SPECT imaging agents is an efficient approach to improve the in vivo properties of NGR peptide.
the cyclic backbone of coNGR-based SPECT tracers is more stable and leads to higher specific uptake in CD13-expressing tissues compared to their disulfide-cycled counterparts.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of a cyclic backbone in the NGR-based imaging agent increases the efficacy of myocardial imaging.
coNGR and co(NGR)-based imaging agents are promising candidates for noninvasive imaging of angiogenesis in the infarcted heart.
the use of a cyclic backbone for NGR peptides increases the efficacy of CD13-targeting agents for postmyocardial infarction angiogenesis imaging.
